audio_script: Before 1920 our world picture was something like this. The stage on which the universe goes is the three-dimensional space of geometry, as described by Euclid, and things change in a medium called time. The elements on the stage are particles, for example the atoms, which have some properties. First, the property of inertia. If a particle is moving it keeps on going in the same direction unless forces act upon it. The second element is forces. There were thought to be of two varieties. First, an enormously complicated detailed kind of interaction force which held the various atoms in different combinations. The other force was a long-range interaction, a smooth and quiet attraction, which varied inversely as the square of the distance and was called gravitation. This law was known and was very simple. Why things remain in motion when they are moving, or why there is a law of gravitation was, of course, not known. A description of nature is what we are concerned with here.

But when we watch the moving clock from outside, we see that the light, in going from mirror to mirror, is really taking a zigzag path, because the rod is moving sideways all the while. So it takes a longer time for light to go from end to end in the moving clock than in the stationary clock. The apparent time between clicks is longer for the moving clock. Not just for this clock. So we must say, in a certain sense, that time itself appears to be slower in a space ship.

header_title: Mass Is a Form of Energy
audio_script: The observation that mass increases with velocity led Einstein to a beautiful suggestion. He said the mass of a body can be expressed more simply. The mass is equal to the total energy content divided by c squared. If we multiply the relativistic mass formula by c squared, we get the total energy of a body. The last term is the ordinary kinetic energy. Einstein interpreted the large constant term, m zero c squared, to be part of the total energy of the body, an intrinsic energy known as the rest energy. Ordinarily these energy changes represent extremely slight changes in mass. But in an atomic bomb of explosive energy equivalent to twenty kilotons of TNT, the dirt after the explosion is lighter by one gram than the initial mass of the reacting material. The released energy had a mass of one gram according to the relationship: delta E equals delta m c squared. This theory of equivalence of mass and energy has been beautifully verified by experiments in which matter is annihilated, converted totally to energy. An electron and a positron come together at rest, each with a rest mass m zero. When they come together they disintegrate and two gamma rays emerge, each with the measured energy of m zero c squared.

audio_script: The space-time region surrounding a given space-time point can be separated into three regions. In one region we have space-like intervals, and in two regions, time-like intervals. Physically, these three regions have an interesting relationship to that point. A physical object or a signal can get from a point in the past region to the event O by moving along at a speed less than the speed of light. Therefore events in this region can affect O, can have an influence on it from the past. Another object can get to O by moving with a certain speed less than c, so if this object were in a space ship and moving, it would be, again, the past of the same space-point. So all points of this region are in the past of O. Therefore this region is sometimes called the affecting past. It is the locus of all events which can affect point O in any way. The region which we can affect from O, we can hit things by shooting bullets out at speeds less than c, this is the world whose future can be affected by us. And we may call that the affecting future. The interesting thing about all the rest of space-time is that we can neither affect it now from O, nor can it affect us now at O, because nothing can go faster than the speed of light.

header_title: Why a Spinning Top Doesn't Fall
audio_script: The origin of the forces which turn us and the chair around as we turn the axis of the gyroscope is a beautiful piece of physics. Figure a wheel spinning rapidly about its axis. Its angular momentum is in that direction. Now suppose we wish to rotate the wheel about a perpendicular axis with a small angular velocity. After a short time the axis has turned to a new position. Since the major part of the angular momentum is due to the spin on the axis, we see that the angular momentum vector has changed. The angular momentum does not change in magnitude, but it does change in direction. So the torque, which is the rate of change of the angular momentum, is Omega cross L zero. Thus, if Omega and L zero are both horizontal, tau is vertical. To produce such a torque, horizontal forces must be applied at the ends of the axle. By our hands. But Newton's third law demands that equal and opposite torques act on us. This causes us to rotate in the opposite sense about the vertical axis. This result can be generalized for a rapidly spinning top. In the familiar case of a spinning top, gravity acting on its center of mass furnishes a torque about the point of contact with the floor. This torque is in the horizontal direction and causes the top to precess with its axis moving in a circular cone about the vertical.

Here is a beautiful idea discovered by Fermat. Out of all possible paths that light might take to get from one point to another, it takes the path which requires the shortest time. Let us first show this is true for a mirror. In the figure are two points A and B and a plane mirror. What is the way to get from A to B in the shortest time with the extra rule that the light has to strike the mirror? If we construct an artificial point B-prime on the other side of the mirror, then the sum of the two distances AE plus EB is equal to AE plus EB-prime. The problem becomes, when is the sum of these two lengths the least? The answer is easy. When the line goes through the correct point as a straight line from A to B-prime. This is equivalent to the statement that the light goes to the mirror in such a way that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Then Fermat asked: what about refraction? For that, light obviously does not use the path of shortest distance. So Fermat tried the idea that it takes the shortest time. If we have a beach and someone falls out of a boat in the water, we can run faster than we can swim. Do we go in a straight line? No. We travel a little greater distance on land to decrease the distance in the water. Following this line of reasoning out, we find that the ratio of the sines of the angles is the ratio of the speeds in the two media. That is Snell's law.

audio_script: Now we imagine a similar experiment with electrons. We make an electron gun which consists of a tungsten wire heated by an electric current. In front of the gun is a wall with two holes in it. Beyond the wall is a backstop, and in front of the backstop, a movable detector. The first thing we notice with our electron experiment is that we hear sharp clicks from the detector. And all clicks are the same. There are no half-clicks. If we count the clicks which arrive in a sufficiently long time and then count again for another equal period, we find that the two numbers are very nearly the same. As we move the detector around, the rate at which the clicks appear is faster or slower, but the size of each click is always the same. The result of our experiment is the interesting curve: the probability of arrival. It is not the sum of the probabilities for the two holes. There is interference. Since the electrons arrive in lumps, each lump has come either through hole one or through hole two. Or has it? This is the heart of quantum mechanics. And it contains the only mystery. We cannot make the mystery go away by explaining how it works. We will just tell you how it works.

Let us try to invent a device which will violate the second law of thermodynamics, that is, a gadget which will generate work from a heat reservoir with everything at the same temperature. We have a box of gas at a certain temperature. Inside there is an axle with vanes in it. Because of the bombardments of gas molecules on the vane, the vane oscillates and jiggles. All we have to do is hook onto the other end of the axle a wheel which can turn only one way, the ratchet and pawl. Then when the shaft tries to jiggle one way it will not turn, and when it jiggles the other it will turn. Then the wheel will slowly turn, and perhaps we might even tie a flea onto a string hanging from a drum on the shaft, and lift the flea. Now let us ask if this is possible. According to Carnot's hypothesis it is impossible. Indeed, if we look closely, the pawl and wheel, both at some temperature, also have Brownian motion. The chance that the system can accumulate enough energy epsilon to get the pawl over the top of the tooth is e to the minus epsilon over kT. The probability that the pawl will accidentally be up is also e to the minus epsilon over kT. So the number of times the pawl is up and the wheel can turn backwards freely is equal to the number of times that we have enough energy to turn it forward when the pawl is down. We get a balance, and the wheel will not go around.

question_text: A muon has a lifetime of 2.2 microseconds in its rest frame. It travels at 0.99c relative to Earth. How far does it travel in the Earth frame before decaying?
audio_script: A muon has a lifetime of two point two microseconds in its rest frame. It travels at ninety-nine percent the speed of light. How far does it travel in the Earth frame before decaying? The key is that the muon's clock runs slow in our frame. First compute the Lorentz factor gamma. Gamma equals one over the square root of one minus v squared over c squared. With v equals zero point nine nine c, we have one minus zero point nine eight zero one, which is zero point zero one nine nine. The square root is about zero point one four one. So gamma is about seven point zero nine. The observed lifetime is gamma times the rest lifetime, which is seven point zero nine times two point two microseconds, about fifteen point six microseconds. The distance is v times the observed time. That is zero point nine nine times three times ten to the eighth meters per second, times fifteen point six times ten to the minus six seconds. That gives about four point six kilometres. So the answer is option B. This is exactly why muons created in the upper atmosphere can reach the ground, even though in their own frame they live only two microseconds.

header_title: Moment of Inertia of a Rod
question_text: A uniform rod of mass M and length L rotates about an axis through one end perpendicular to its length. What is its moment of inertia?
audio_script: A uniform rod of mass M and length L rotates about an axis through one end perpendicular to its length. What is its moment of inertia? The moment of inertia about an axis is the sum of the masses times the square of the distance from the axis. So we must sum all the masses times the x-distances squared. If we divide the rod into small elements of length dx, the corresponding element of mass is M dx over L. So the moment of inertia is the integral from zero to L of x squared times M dx over L. That is M over L times the integral of x squared dx, which gives M over L times L cubed over three. So I equals M L squared over three. That is option B. Notice how the position of the axis matters enormously. If we had chosen an axis through the centre of the rod instead, we would get M L squared over twelve, which is four times smaller. That is the parallel-axis theorem at work. A rod is easier to spin about its centre than about its end, because the mass is closer to the axis on average.
